races.long_description: Senator Tommy Tuberville, the Republican firebrand and former Auburn football coach, is facing Doug Jones, the Democrat he ousted in 2020. Mr. Tuberville’s campaign has been defined by his alliance with President Trump and a steady drumbeat of anti-Muslim and anti-immigrant messaging, while Mr. Jones leaned on his Senate record and civil rights work.

Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, a former state lawmaker, is trying to become Alaska’s youngest governor ever and its first Democratic one since 1998. Under Alaska’s top-four ranked-choice voting system, he faces three Republicans: Bernadette Wilson, owner of a garbage collection company; Treg Taylor, a former attorney general; and Dave Bronson, a former Anchorage mayor. Ms. Wilson has President Trump’s endorsement.

Gov. Katie Hobbs of Arizona, the Democratic incumbent, is fighting to keep control of the desert battleground’s highest office. Ms. Hobbs, a moderate, is facing Representative Andy Biggs, a Trump-endorsed former chair of the far-right House Freedom Caucus who’s backed by Turning Point USA.

Gov. Sarah Huckabee Sanders, a Republican, is heavily favored to win a second term. Ms. Sanders, who served as President Trump’s press secretary during his first term, is facing Fred Love, a Democratic state senator.
Xavier Becerra, a Democrat who served as secretary of health and human services in the Biden administration, is favored to defeat Steve Hilton, a former Fox News host endorsed by President Trump.

Colorado, a onetime swing state that has veered to the left, is expected to elect Phil Weiser, the state’s Democratic attorney general, as its next governor. Republicans were deeply divided over their own candidate, Victor Marx, a ministry leader and political neophyte.

Gov. Ned Lamont, a Democrat, is seeking a third consecutive term, a feat accomplished only once before in the state. His Republican challenger, Ryan Fazio, a state senator from Greenwich, is grappling with fierce political headwinds. No one in his party has won a statewide election in 20 years.

Byron Donalds, the Republican backed by President Trump, is vying to continue the party’s dominance in the governor’s mansion. A victory would make him Florida’s first Black governor. He faces David Jolly, a former Republican congressman who became a Democrat last year. No Democrat has held the governorship in Florida since the late 1990s.

Rick Jackson, a health care executive, is aiming to hold the governorship for Republicans in politically mixed Georgia. He is facing Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat and a former mayor of Atlanta. The Republican incumbent, Gov. Brian Kemp, was barred by term limits from running again.

Gov. Josh Green of Hawaii, a Democrat who led his state during the Maui wildfires in 2023, is heavily favored to win a second term in a place where Republicans are rarely competitive in statewide races. Gary Cordery, a businessman, is the Republican nominee.
Gov. Brad Little, a Republican, is seeking a third term in a reliably conservative state. Terri Pickens, a lawyer, is the Democratic nominee.

Gov. JB Pritzker, a billionaire Democrat who is believed to be weighing a run for president, is seeking a third term in his solidly Democratic state. Mr. Pritzker, a vocal critic of President Trump, is facing a rematch of his 2022 race with Darren Bailey, a Republican former state senator.

In a state that has been controlled by Republicans for close to a decade, a surprisingly competitive race for governor has unfolded between Rob Sand, the Democratic state auditor, and Zach Lahn, a Republican supported by the MAHA movement.

Republicans see Kansas as an opportunity to flip the governorship on an otherwise foreboding electoral map. Ty Masterson, the Republican nominee and president of the Kansas Senate, has aligned himself with President Trump. State Senator Cindy Holscher, who emerged from a fractious Democratic primary, is trying to hold the seat for her party.

Hannah Pingree, a Democrat and former Maine House speaker, has maintained a steady lead in polls over Bobby Charles, a conservative Republican. The winner will succeed Gov. Janet Mills, a term-limited Democrat whose conflict with President Trump raised her national profile.

Gov. Wes Moore, a Democrat and possible future presidential candidate, is a heavy favorite in his bid for a second term. He is facing a rematch with Dan Cox, a Republican former state legislator who lost to Mr. Moore by a large margin four years ago.

Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat and a vocal critic of President Trump, is seeking a second term in her solidly Democratic state. Mike Minogue, a former medical technology executive with conservative views, is the Republican nominee.

Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson is trying to keep the governor’s office in Democratic hands for a third straight term. She faces Representative John James, a Republican from suburban Detroit, in a state where voters swing regularly between parties.

Senator Amy Klobuchar, a Democrat, entered the governor’s race early this year after Gov. Tim Walz suspended his campaign for a third term amid a scandal over social services fraud. She is favored to defeat Lisa Demuth, the Republican speaker of the Minnesota House.

Gov. Jim Pillen, a Republican, is facing a surprisingly competitive re-election race in a state that has not elected a Democrat as governor in more than 30 years but where many voters are frustrated with federal agricultural policies. His opponent, former State Senator Lynne Walz, has pitched herself to voters as a different kind of Democrat, often noting her Christian faith and her childhood on a hog farm.

Joe Lombardo, a relatively moderate Republican, is looking to win re-election in one of the nation’s most competitive races for governor. He faces the state’s attorney general, Democrat Aaron Ford, who has sought to tie Mr. Lombardo to President Trump. Mr. Ford would be Nevada’s first Black governor.

Gov. Kelly Ayotte, a Republican who served in the U.S. Senate, is seeking re-election, while her challenger, Cinde Warmington, a Democratic lawyer and former lobbyist, argues that Ms. Ayotte would enable “more Trump chaos” in a second term.

Deb Haaland, the former Democratic congresswoman and interior secretary, is looking to become the nation’s first female Native American governor. A Republican former mayor, Gregg Hull, is mounting a long-shot challenge notable for the unusual promise he made at its outset: No negative campaigning.

After winning by a closer-than-expected margin four years ago, Gov. Kathy Hochul is hoping that anger with President Trump will turn out Democratic voters and help her comfortably secure a second term over her Republican opponent, Bruce Blakeman, the Nassau County executive.

In an expensive and markedly bitter race, Vivek Ramaswamy, who made millions in pharmaceutical start-ups and briefly ran for president in 2024, is running against Dr. Amy Acton, who was the state’s chief public health officer in the early days of the Covid pandemic.

Mike Mazzei, a former state senator, emerged from a competitive Republican primary with President Trump’s endorsement and is favored to hold the open seat for his party. But Democrats, whose candidates are usually trounced in statewide races, have invested in the race and expressed hope that their nominee, State Representative Cyndi Munson, could be competitive.

In a rematch of 2022, Democratic incumbent Tina Kotek faces Christine Drazan, a conservative Republican state legislator. Ms. Kotek’s low approval rating and the state’s slow recovery from the pandemic have made this a closer campaign than the state’s demographics would suggest.

Josh Shapiro, a Democrat and a potential 2028 presidential contender, is running for re-election against Stacy Garrity, the state treasurer and a retired colonel in the U.S. Army Reserve. With healthy approval numbers statewide, Mr. Shapiro has kept a formidable lead in the polls.

Helena Foulkes, a Democrat who is a former CVS executive, defeated Gov. Dan McKee in her party’s primary to establish herself as a strong favorite in the general election. Her opponents include Aaron Guckian, a Republican, and Ken Block, a businessman running as an independent.

Gov. Larry Rhoden, a Republican, emerged from a competitive primary as a strong favorite to be elected to a full term. Mr. Rhoden, who had been lieutenant governor, ascended to the state’s highest office last year when former Gov. Kristi Noem joined President Trump’s cabinet. He is facing Dan Ahlers, a Democrat who previously served in the State Legislature.

Senator Marsha Blackburn, a Trump ally, is the front-runner to become Tennessee’s first female governor. She faces a number of challengers, including Jerri Green, a Democratic Memphis councilwoman. There are also two surprisingly robust independent challenges from Lauren Pinkston, an academic, and David Hatley, a businessman.

Greg Abbott, the well-moneyed, longtime governor of Texas, is up against Gina Hinojosa, a state lawmaker who has pulled ahead in the polls in recent weeks. No matter the outcome, it will be record-setting: A win for Mr. Abbott would mean a fourth term as governor, a first in Texas history; a win for Ms. Hinojosa would mean the state’s first Hispanic governor.
Gov. Phil Scott, a moderate Republican seeking a sixth term, is facing Amanda Janoo, a progressive Democrat and a political newcomer whose campaign has picked up unexpected momentum.

Representative Tom Tiffany, a Republican with close ties to President Trump, is facing David Crowley, a Democrat and the Milwaukee County executive. Mr. Crowley is hoping to keep the seat in Democratic hands and help his party win a trifecta in Wisconsin.

State Senator Eric Barlow, a Republican who defeated a candidate endorsed by President Trump in the primary election, is widely expected to hold the governorship for his party. Ken Casner, the Democratic nominee, is a military veteran who runs a retail shop and cafe.

content.text: In downtown Atlanta, Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia congratulated Senator Jon Ossoff, “his brother from another mother,” as Warnock put it. “Jon Ossoff and I are ready to get into some more good trouble on behalf of the people of Georgia,” Warnock said in an homage to the late congressman and civil rights activist John Lewis, a mentor to both senators. Then Warnock turned to the victory of Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms, another Democrat.

“I had to facetime my 10-year-old daughter and tell her that for the first time ever in the history of our republic, we have a Black woman who is a governor,” Warnock said. “That’s good news for all of our little girls, and indeed for all of our children, because every child ought to have a path.”

An election-night watch party for the South Carolina Republican Party in Columbia, S.C., started out upbeat, with guests posing for pictures and saying that they expected Senator Darline Graham to pull through her close Senate race. But the mood curdled as it became clear that Dr. Annie Andrews, Graham’s Democratic opponent, would deliver a stunning upset in the deep-red state.

Guests turned their chairs away from tables full of pork sliders to face billboard-sized TV screens that were full of disappointing news for their party. Some called Ubers. Leeds Barroll, 74, lawyer who donated to Graham’s campaign, said he was surprised that the race was not closer. “I thought she would have been a great senator,” he said of Graham. Several attendees repeated the same word over and over: “Wow.”

Bob Brooks, a Democratic retired firefighter and union leader who spoke candidly during his campaign of relying on public housing and food stamps after his family’s home burned down, flipped a House seat in Pennsylvania’s Lehigh Valley, according to The Associated Press, handing Democrats a crucial victory in a competitive district.

He unseated Representative Ryan Mackenzie, a Republican who flipped the Seventh Congressional District two years ago. Brooks focused his campaign on Mackenzie’s support of President Trump’s agenda, which Brooks argued had driven up costs. His victory appeared to vindicate Democrats’ efforts to appeal to working-class voters; Brooks will be among the few House Democrats who did not graduate from college.

A number of Maine’s 400-plus localities have finished counting their votes, and Susan Collins is improving on President Trump’s margin in 2024 in many of them — a sharp departure from Republican fortunes elsewhere tonight. Collins, though, is in a unique position as the only Republican incumbent running in a state the president lost in the last three elections. To keep her seat, she will need to perform well across most of the state.

“This is a mandate to deliver big change,” Representative Greg Casar, a Texas Democrat who leads the Congressional Progressive Caucus, said in a statement as returns continued to roll in showing favorable results for Democrats. “Tonight is the beginning of the end of the Trump era. Tomorrow we begin building the better world that comes next.”

The election of Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democrat, as Georgia governor could have some impact on the 2028 presidential race. Some Democrats are hoping that Senator Jon Ossoff, another Georgia Democrat who won tonight, or Senator Raphael Warnock will make bids for the White House in 2028.

If Ossoff or Warnock were to become president, Democrats could rest easy that the party would keep the vacated Senate seat, at least for a while — because a Governor Bottoms would appoint a temporary successor until a special election could be held.

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic minority leader from New York, celebrated with his staff in Washington while watching election results roll in as more candidates in his party won House seats.

The loss by Darline Graham is, among other things, a black eye for the data-center industry, which made a late play to try to help her with the first spending of its kind. The data-center industry set up a new super PAC this fall and the group
chose Graham as its first candidate to back
. The politics of data centers are going to remain dicey going forward.

Democrats are making significant inroads into Republican territory in their battle for control of the House, flipping Republican-held seats in northern New Jersey and western North Carolina, while picking up an open seat held by an outgoing Republican in the Lexington area of Kentucky.

And the night is still early, with other G.O.P. districts appearing in jeopardy. Democrats seem to be finding opportunities to expand the electoral map beyond their most obvious pickup targets, raising the stakes for Republicans as more competitive races are decided.

over Scott Colom, a Democrat, with about half of the vote counted. The race is now considered a tossup, according to our estimates, with a disproportionate number of votes left to be counted from the Mississippi Delta, the state’s most heavily Black and Democratic region.

A tranche of ballots that election officials in Westchester County, N.Y., were unable to process because of difficulties with the ballot-scanning machines will be counted tomorrow starting at 11 a.m. and will continue until they are finished, according to a consent order that a State Supreme Court justice just signed. Lawyers for the State Democratic and State Republican Party, endorsed the plan, and the ballots will be counted under supervision of lawyers from both sides.
This
counting delay may end up affecting

how soon a result is known in one of the most competitive House races in the country, which is taking place outside New York City. Representative Mike Lawler, the incumbent Republican, is facing Cait Conley, a Democrat.

Rebecca Bennett, a Democrat in New Jersey, has become the first Democrat to unseat a Republican incumbent this year, defeating Representative Tom Kean Jr. She is among a cohort of military veterans whom Democrats have recruited and supported in 2026. “Female veterans and women with national security backgrounds are uniquely positioned at being able to flip seats red to blue,”
she told me last year

Michigan has its first completed county, Luce, a small rural area in the state’s Upper Peninsula. The county has shifted around five percentage points toward Dr. Abdul El-Sayed compared with the 2024 presidential election, a smaller shift than in many other competitive states tonight. But President Trump won Michigan by under two percentage points, so El-Sayed does not require as drastic of a shift to win.
Michigan Election Results ›

Dan Osborn’s current lead in the Nebraska Senate race will almost certainly shrink as the night goes on. The state’s biggest counties were some of the first to report, and the remaining votes, which are largely from rural counties, are expected to be favorable to Pete Ricketts, the Republican incumbent.

Still, Osborn is doing slightly better than he did in his ultimately unsuccessful 2024 campaign against Deb Fischer. At this point in the night in 2024, Osborn led by a little over nine percentage points; this year, he’s ahead by more than 13.

updates.headline: Update from Leanne Abraham and Arfa Momin

content.text: There are so many questions right now about what comes next, across Washington and across the Republican Party. The MAGA movement will still exist. But the notion that this is a durable coalition that will outlast President Trump, as his advisers had hoped, has suffered some blows tonight.

Sherrod Brown has run for Senate in Ohio three times in the last eight years. Between his 2018 and 2024 re-election campaigns, eight counties that had voted Democratic flipped to Republicans, helping contribute to his defeat. This year, based on the votes reported so far, five of those counties have swung back in his favor.

In Texas, the Houston area is a key part to any statewide victory as it contains roughly a quarter of the state’s voters. In Harris County, which includes Houston, James Talarico is leading Ken Paxton by more than 30 percentage points, with about three-quarters of the expected vote in. By comparison, Kamala Harris carried the county by only six percentage points in 2024, and Beto O’Rourke carried it by about 17 points in 2018.

Talarico is also seeing shifts his way in Montgomery County, which is just north of Harris and is historically a Republican stronghold. President Trump carried that county by 45 percentage points in 2024. With about 70 percent of the expected vote having been reported, Paxton leads Talarico by a more modest 21 points.

The Tennessee governor’s race remains surprisingly close between Senator Marsha Blackburn, a Republican, and Jerri Green, a Memphis councilwoman and the Democratic nominee. David Hatley, a conservative-leaning independent, has siphoned away more than 100,000 votes, making it a closer-than-expected contest so far.
Tennessee Governor Election Results ›

The Democrats are on track to win the national House popular vote by 12 percentage points, according to our estimates. That would be the largest popular victory in the national congressional vote for either party since 1982 — back when Democrats ran up the score nationwide with overwhelming support in the South.

James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas, is heading toward victory, according to our estimates, with a greater than 95 percent chance to win. A Democratic victory of any size is extraordinary in Texas, which has symbolized the Republican Party’s hold on the heartland for a generation, but Talarico is on track for a jaw-dropping margin given the state’s conservative tilt.

Stefany Shaheen, a Democrat, won the First Congressional District in New Hampshire, defeating Anthony DiLorenzo, a Trump-endorsed businessman. The district is a classic House battleground that has flip-flopped between Republican and Democratic control five times since 2002.
At the Democratic watch party in Manchester, Shaheen was joined by her family onstage, including her mother, the retiring Senator Jeanne Shaheen.
New Hampshire First Congressional District Election Results ›

One of the first counties to largely complete its reporting in Kansas’ Senate race is Seward, a rural county with the highest percentage of Hispanic voters in the state. Adam Hamilton, the Democrat, won the county by double digits after President Trump won it by 40 percentage points just two years ago. The shift is one of many in majority-Hispanic areas around the country tonight.

Byron Donalds gave a short victory speech after voters elected him Florida’s next governor. He praised David Jolly, his Democratic opponent, for a hard-fought campaign. Donalds said he had also spoken to President Trump by phone. “Mr. Trump, here in Florida, we are still red,” Donalds said to raucous applause.

The Republican nominee for governor in Georgia, Rick Jackson, a billionaire health care executive, conceded defeat to Keisha Lance Bottoms, a Democratic former Atlanta mayor, and delivered a concession speech laced with prayer, optimism and thanks to friends, family and “associates of Jackson Healthcare.”
“Tonight the voters spoke, and I respect their decision,” Jackson said. “Keisha Lance Bottoms deserves our gratitude, congratulations and our prayers as she prepares to take office.”

The mood at the watch party in Austin for Gov. Greg Abbott of Texas was livelier earlier, when an ’80s cover band was performing, but when the band took a break, supporters of the Republican incumbent were refreshing election results on their phones, which show Abbott’s challenger, Gina Hinojosa, with an early lead with about 54 percent of the vote in.

Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, a Democrat, addressed a crowd of hundreds in downtown Atlanta after winning his re-election bid. “In sweeping and decisive victories,” he said, “the American people have rebuked the depravity, corruption, and incompetence of the failed lame duck President Donald J. Trump.”
He added: “While the wealthy and well-lobbied feast on inside information and official favors, America’s forgotten families are treated to systemic corporate disrespect and official indifference.”

The Democrats have a greater than 95 percent chance to win the Senate, according to our estimates. A final call may not come for hours, but Democrats have either won or are likely to win the four Republican-held states they need to take the chamber: Texas, South Carolina, North Carolina and Ohio. Democrats have additional opportunities in Kansas, Maine, Iowa and Alaska, where they are favored to prevail should another state fall through.

In the Kansas Senate race, Adam Hamilton, the Democratic candidate and megachurch pastor, has a lead with around 40 percent of the expected vote having been reported. While that advantage is expected to decrease as more votes are reported, Hamilton has greatly outperformed Kamala Harris’s 2024 margins statewide. Rural counties such as Ellis County, Labette County and Reno County have shifted close to 20 percentage points to the left.

A large number of votes are still to come in Johnson County, the largest in the state by population. The early vote there showed a large shift toward Hamilton, with the Democrat leading the county by 36 points.

One thing Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia won’t say as he congratulates Keisha Lance Bottoms for becoming the state’s Democratic governor-elect is that with his resounding Senate victory, he helped lift her and other Democrats down the ballot. Ossoff invited Bottoms to one of his big rallies as far back as May and also more recently, including to a rally that featured former President Barack Obama.

Democrats at the official watch party for the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee are particularly excited about the fact that Representative Richard Hudson, Republican of North Carolina and the chairman of the National Republican Campaign Committee, is currently trailing his Democratic opponent.
North Carolina Ninth Congressional District Election Results ›

Virginia voters have approved a measure that restores the right to vote for people convicted of felonies upon their release, The Associated Press reported. The measure also limits the state’s ban on voting for people deemed mentally incompetent by a court, requiring that a court specifically finds that a person is unable to understand the act of voting.
James Talarico now has a 90 percent chance to win the
Senate race in Texas

for Democrats, according to our estimates. No Election Day vote has been counted yet, but his overwhelming advantage in the early vote means that his Republican rival, Ken Paxton, would need extraordinary turnout on Election Day to prevail.

David Jolly, the Democratic nominee for governor of Florida, just conceded. Addressing supporters in Tampa’s convention center, he said, “Yes, we have lost this election tonight, but we have not lost the fight in any of us.” He notes just how big of a night Democrats are having elsewhere. “This is a big night across the country,” he said, adding that “Americans are exercising the democracy that has been pent-up for a very long time.”

The Democrat Annie Andrews continues to lead in South Carolina, in part because she has managed to make strong inroads into blue-collar communities that have been strong supporters of President Trump.

Three South Carolina counties where white residents without college degrees make up a majority of the population have finished counting their votes. Each of those counties have shifted by more than 20 percentage points toward Andrews, compared with the 2024 presidential election.
More broadly, South Carolina counties that voted for Trump in 2024 swung to the left by an average of about 21 percentage points.
Virginia voters have approved a ballot measure repealing language in the state Constitution prohibiting marriage between same-sex couples, The Associated Press reported.

The ban has been unenforceable since the 2015 Supreme Court ruling that established same-sex marriage as a national right, but would come back into effect if that ruling were overturned. The measure establishes a right to marriage between consenting adults “regardless of sex, gender or race.”

In Jacksonville, Fla., Angie Nixon has just given a rousing concession speech in the Florida Senate race, in which she indicated she would not be fading into the background in state politics. “I’m an organizer, not a politician,” she said. “And organizers don’t quit on the mission because one option closes.” She added: “We have built something that no election outcome can take away from us.”

In South Carolina, Annie Andrews, the Democratic nominee, has a chance to flip a Senate seat that has been held by a Republican since Strom Thurmond changed parties in 1964. She has done well throughout the state, shifting the vote more than 20 percentage points to the left in about a dozen counties that have largely completed reporting. She could also be the first woman ever elected to the U.S. Senate from the state, since Senator Darline Graham, her Republican opponent, was appointed to the seat.

content.text: In Texas, several heavily Hispanic counties across the state have reported a substantial share of their votes. James Talarico is running ahead of Kamala Harris’s 2024 margins in all of them. These include border counties in the Rio Grande Valley, like Cameron, which President Trump flipped in 2024, as well as urban counties like Bexar and El Paso, which Harris won in 2024 by much smaller margins.

Annie Andrews, a Democrat, is edging toward a stunning victory over Senator Darline Graham, a Republican, in the South Carolina Senate race, with a greater than 95 percent chance to win, according to our estimates. This is not a projection, but an Andrews victory would greatly narrow the Republican path to retaining control of the Senate.
The mood inside President Trump’s watch event in the East Room is fairly lackluster and devoid of energy, according to people on hand.

Trump’s history of election night events in that room is not stellar: In 2018, he huddled with Mike Pence’s adviser Nick Ayers, who the president wanted to make his own White House chief of staff, before Ayers turned it down. That night, several high-profile Republican elected officials stayed away from the White House. And 2020 was marked by the president’s infamous declaration that “frankly, we did win” the election, after Arizona was called for President Joseph R. Biden Jr.
